text: Good evening. Ruth Hale, Elm Street Library. I run the adult programs, which mostly means I set out chairs. $ I used to set out twenty for the citizenship class. Since the new federal rules I set out ten, and some weeks I put five back. People have stopped writing their address on a sign-up sheet. Patients wait at home until it's an ambulance. This week a man was taken at a checkpoint on Route 9 on his way to work, and his wife came to the library first, because that is where she reads her letters. $ So I'll say it plainly: these policies are wrong, and they are meant to divide this town. They won't, as long as we keep showing up for each other.

_turns to the moderator_ You asked what the next governor should do first. Keep the state troopers out of the federal checks, and say so out loud, so people stop skipping the clinic. Pay for interpreters at the state clinics instead of fighting the rule. $ Then fund the plain things that hold a town together: library hours in the evening, books in the languages people actually read, a room for the health fair, flyers for the block-party potluck in five languages with the date in big numbers. $ And come to {homeCenter} when they invite you, not only when there's a camera. I go. You eat well, and you learn who your neighbours are. That's most of the job.

Good evening. Ruth Hale, Elm Street Library, adult programs. $ For six years I asked for two lines in my budget: more English sections, and money for phone interpreters. This year Washington paid for both. With the backlog plan, people in my citizenship class may get their interviews before their grandchildren graduate. I'm glad, and I'm not shy about saying so. $ But a federal rule is a piece of paper until somebody at a front desk picks up the phone. This state has said it won't enforce the interpreter rule at its own clinics. So the work is still ours: the clinic desk, the library desk, {homeCenter}, all of us, in every language this neighbourhood speaks.

_turns to the moderator_ What should the next governor do first? Enforce the interpreter rule at the state clinics, and stop calling it a burden. $ Then put money where people already gather. Our new shelf has books in eleven languages because families from {homeCenter} sent us the list. I went to their {homeFestival} celebration to ask what to add, and came home with forty titles and too much to eat. $ I'd like the next governor to come to one of those nights, and to our block-party potluck. Not to give a speech. To sit at a table between two families who have never met, and pass the food. That's how a town turns into one town.
That's it exactly. Say it again on Thursday, in both your languages, and I'll make sure the new families are at your table.
I hear you, and English matters; I teach it. $ I just don't think anybody has to stop being who they are to learn it.
People want somewhere that feels like home, and I understand that. I'd only ask you to leave a door open, so the rest of us can find it.
Listening is a fine place to start. Come and listen at the potluck; the food's better than tonight's coffee.
Thank you for getting up there. It's harder than it looks, and you made it sound like a conversation.
